synopsis: RAND’s Driving to Safety, by Kalra and Paddock (report RR-1478-RC), was published in April 2016 and supplies the booklet’s statistical reason for pursuing virtual testing [f6920, f15817]. Chapter 9 and the glossary agree that demonstrating autonomous road-vehicle reliability requires hundreds of millions, and sometimes hundreds of billions, of driven miles—distances that existing fleets would need tens or hundreds of years to accumulate [f6921, f15812, f14264]. Showing a fatality rate no worse than the human benchmark of 1.09 fatalities per 100 million miles requires 275 million failure-free miles at 95% confidence [f6662, f6922, f15813]. Demonstrating a 20% fatality-rate improvement requires about 11 billion miles; Chapter 9 specifies 80% statistical power and, in its fuller statement, 95% confidence, while the glossary omits those statistical qualifiers [f6663, f6923, f15814]. These figures concern autonomous road vehicles; the supplied facts do not quantify corresponding mileage requirements for heavy off-road machines [f6921, f6922, f6923].
